---
title: Observable state
description: "How an Arkitekt app publishes what it is doing instead of answering questions about it: one owner per state, changes sent as numbered JSON Patch updates, snapshots, a journal you can replay, and watchers that never poll."
type: concept
---

A device app knows where its stage is. Instead of waiting to be asked, it **publishes** that
knowledge, and everyone who cares watches it: the UI, a blok, a workflow deciding whether it is
safe to dispense.

```python
@app.state
class Stage:
    x_um: float = 0.0
    moving: bool = False


@app.action
def move_to(x_um: float, stage: Stage, task: Task) -> None:
    """Move To"""
    with task.updating(stage):      # one update
        stage.x_um = x_um
        stage.moving = False
```

Assigning to a field is all it takes. The runtime turns the change into JSON Patch operations, gives
the state its next **revision**, and sends it as one update to the server, which passes it on to
everyone watching.

## The patterns

Three well-known patterns meet here:

- **Publish/subscribe (observer).** The app publishes, watchers subscribe. Nobody polls, and the
  app does not know or care who is watching. This is why there are no getter actions: see
  [Anti-patterns](/docs/build/anti-patterns#getters).
- **Single writer.** A state has exactly one owner, the agent that declares it. Others read it and
  ask the owner to change it by calling an action. Locks on the state (`required_locks=`) make sure
  only one task commands it at a time.
- **Event sourcing with snapshots.** Every update is numbered, recorded in the agent's journal and
  in the server's history, and every 60th revision also carries a full snapshot of the app's states.
  The state at any moment is the last snapshot plus the updates after it. That is what lets a blok
  show the state as it was at an earlier moment.

## What it buys

- **One truth per device.** Every UI, script and workflow sees the same value, from the one process
  that knows it. A UI keeping its own copy is the thing this replaces
  ([Anti-patterns](/docs/build/anti-patterns#ui-state)).
- **No polling.** Ten watchers cost the app nothing more than one.
- **Guards for workflows.** A workflow can require that a device's state holds before acting on it
  (`task.guard`), because the state is published where the workflow can see it.
- **A history.** Because updates are numbered and recorded, what a device was doing is part of the
  record, next to the tasks that changed it.

## What it costs

- **Every update is a frame.** Nothing is merged or dropped: an assignment in a tight loop is a
  stream of frames, each stored. State must be **small** (no arrays) and **slow** (written when it
  changes meaningfully, at a rate someone can act on). Live data goes through a stream. See
  [Anti-patterns](/docs/build/anti-patterns#frequency).
- **There is latency.** An update travels from the agent through the server to each watcher. State
  is for knowing what is going on and deciding on it, not for closing a control loop.
